[Cite as Sorensen v. Hellas, 2026-Ohio-4546.] 
 
IN THE OHIO COURT OF APPEALS 
FIFTH APPELLATE DISTRICT 
DELAWARE COUNTY, OHIO 
 
 
SORENSEN CONSTRUCTION, INC.  
 
Plaintiff-Appellant/Cross-Appellee 
 
-vs- 
 
HELLAS INVESTMENTS, LTD. 
 
Defendant-Appellee/Cross-Appellant 
 
Case Nos. 26 CAE 07 0071 & 26 CAE 07 0073 
 
Opinion and Judgment Entry 
 
Appeal from the Delaware County Court of 
Common Pleas, Case No. 25CV H 01 112 
 
Judgment: Affirmed 
 
Date of Judgment Entry: November 16, 2026  
 
 
 
 
BEFORE: William B. Hoffman; Craig R. Baldwin; Kevin W. Popham, Judges 
 
APPEARANCES: Dave Lackey, Sybert, Rhoad, Lackey & Swisher, LLC, for Plaintiff-
Appellant; Bryan M. Pritikin, Roetzel & Andress, LPA, for Defendant-Appellee. 
 
 
 
Hoffman, P.J. 
 
{¶1} In Delaware App. No. 26CAE070071, plaintiff-appellant/cross-appellee 
Sorensen Construction, Inc. (“Sorensen Construction”) appeals the April 23, 2026 Judgment 
Entry entered by the Delaware County Court of Common Pleas, which denied its motion for 
summary judgment and granted summary judgment in favor of defendant-appellee/cross-
appellant Hellas Investments LTD (“Hellas”), and the July 9, 2026 Judgment Entry, which 
approved and adopted the magistrate’s June 24, 2026 decision awarding damages to Hellas. 
In Delaware App. No. 26CAE070073, Hellas appeals the July 9, 2026 Judgment Entry, which 
failed to award it attorney fees incurred prior to January 27, 2025. 
 
 
STATEMENT OF THE CASE AND FACTS 
{¶2} John Vlahos (“Vlahos”) contacted Don Sorensen and requested Sorensen 
Construction perform renovation work on real property located at 7575 Riverside Drive, 
Powell, Ohio (“the Property”). Don Sorensen, Sorensen Construction’s 30(B)(5) 
representative, described the work as a “complete renovation” of the Property, “from the 
ground up.” Deposition of Don Sorensen, pp. 12, 14, 16, 27, attached as Exhibit 3 to Hellas’ 
November 18, 2025 Motion for Summary Judgment. Don Sorensen testified Hellas never 
contracted with Sorensen Construction. Vlahos and Don Sorensen discussed the oral contract 
regarding the work at the Property, but a contract never materialized in writing. 
{¶3} At the time Vlahos engaged Sorensen Construction, the Property was owned 
by Hellas, a single-member entity controlled entirely by the John Vlahos Trust.  The trustee 
of the John Vlahos Trust was Vlahos. Hellas was “[b]asically. . . a holding company for th e 
rentals that [Vlahos] had.”  Deposition of John A. VanSickle, p. 11, attached as Exhibit 1 to 
Hellas’ November 18, 2025 Motion for Summary Judgment. 
{¶4} Sorensen Construction performed some of the renovation work and obtained a 
certificate of occupancy on March 24, 2023.   After the certificate of occupancy was acquired, 
Sorensen Construction was denied access to the Property and was not permitted to perfo rm 
any additional work on the Property. Vlahos placed tools and equipment belonging to 
Sorensen Construction outside the residence.  At that point, Vlahos had paid $292,000, 
directly to Sorensen Construction and an additional $72,000, directly to subcontra ctors and 
suppliers.  According to Sorensen Construction, Vlahos, however, refused to pay the 20% 
contractor’s fee. Sorensen Construction subsequently filed a mechanic’s lien against the 
 
 
Property, claiming it was owed $32,250. When Don Sorensen attempted to file the mechanic’s 
lien, he learned the Property was owned by Hellas. 
{¶5} On June 30, 2023, Sorensen Construction filed a complaint against Hellas and 
Vlahos for, inter alia, breach of contract and unjust enrichment, and seeking damages in the 
amount of $32,250 (“Prior Action”). Vlahos passed away on August 14, 2023, and Sorensen 
Construction dismissed its claims against him individually. Sorensen Construction filed a 
motion for summary judgment on January 22, 2024, which the trial court denied.  Depositions 
were taken and discovery exchanged.  Sorensen Construction filed a motio n for partial 
summary judgment on November 20, 2024. Hellas filed a memorandum in opposition on 
December 17, 2024.  After the trial court denied its motion for partial summary judgment, 
Sorensen Construction filed a notice of dismissal on January 27, 2025. 
{¶6} Also on January 27, 2025, Sorensen Construction filed the complaint in the 
instant action for breach of contract and unjust enrichment, and seeking damages in the 
amount of $72,800.00 (“Refiled Action”).  The facts and issues in the Prior Action  were 
identical to the facts and issues in the Refiled Action. On March 14, 2025, Hellas filed an 
answer and counterclaim for slander of title/falsification, quiet title, and declaratory 
judgment. Sorensen Construction filed a reply to Hellas’ counterclaim on April 3, 2025. 
{¶7} Sorensen Construction filed a motion for summary judgment on November 14, 
2025.  Hellas filed a motion for summary judgment on November 18, 2025. Via Judgment 
Entry filed April 23, 2026, the trial court denied Sorensen Construction’s motion for summary 
judgment and granted Hellas’ motion for summary judgment.  
{¶8} In denying Sorensen Construction’s motion for summary judgment on its 
claims, the trial court found a valid, enforceable contract did not exist between Sorensen 
 
 
Construction and Hellas; therefore, a breach of contract could not occur. The trial court 
further found Sorensen Construction failed to provide sufficient evidence to establish Hellas 
was unjustly enriched or that Sorensen Construction suffered any loss.  The trial court granted 
summary judgment in favor of Hellas on its counterclaims, finding Sorensen Construction 
filed the mechanic’s lien on the Property without providing a “bona fide and evidence-backed 
way to show the total cost of the Project;” without  Hellas “being a party to the oral contract 
and without any accounting on whether the Project had been paid if full.” April 23, 2026 
Judgment Entry at p. 10.  The trial court concluded Sorensen Construction filed the 
mechanic’s lien with reckless or wanton disregard for its falsity. The trial court found the 
invalid mechanic’s lien created a cloud of Hellas’ title ; therefore, Hellas was entitled to 
summary judgment on its slander of title claim.  In addition, the trial court determined, 
because the Property was unique and Hellas had no adequate remedy at law through which 
to remove the cloud and clear the title, Hellas was entitled to summary judgment on its claims 
for quiet title and declaratory judgment. 
{¶9} The magistrate conducted a hearing on the issue of damages related to Hellas’ 
slander of title claim on June 3, 2026.  Via decision filed June 24, 2026, the magistrate 
awarded damages to Hellas in the amount $111,714.00.  The total damage award consisted 
of $28,796.00, for work performed by Jon VanSickle; $78,518.00, in attorney fees from 
January 27, 2026, to date; and $4,400.00, in expert fees. Sorensen Construction filed 
objections to the magistrate’s June 24, 2026 decision, arguing the award was excessiv e as 
Hellas failed to mitigate damages as it could have filed an application pursuant to R.C. 
1311.11(C) to discharge the lien. Hellas also filed objections to the magistrate’s decision, 
 
 
asserting it should have been awarded attorney fees for work performed in defending the Prior 
Action.  
{¶10} Via Judgment Entry filed July 9, 2026, the trial court overruled the parties’ 
respective objections, and approved and adopted the magistrate’s June 24, 2026 decision as 
judgment of the court. 
{¶11} In Delaware App. No. 26CAE070071, Sorensen Construction appeals the trial 
court’s April 23, 2026, and July 9, 2026 Judgment Entries, raising the following assignments 
of error: 
 
I. THE TRIAL COURT ERRED IN DENYING PLAINTIFF -
APPELLANT’S MOTION FOR SUMMARY JUDGMENT ON ITS 
BREACH OF CONTRACT CLAIM. 
II. THE TRIAL COURT ERRED IN DENYING PLAINTIFF -
APPELLANT’S MOTION FOR SUMMARY JUDGMENT ON ITS 
UNJUST ENRICHMENT CLAIM (AS AN ALTERNATIVE TO ITS 
BREACH OF CONTRACT CLAIM). 
III. THE TRIAL COURT ERRED IN GRANTING DEFENDANT -
APPELLEE’S MOTION FOR SUMMARY JUDGMENT ON ITS 
SLANDER OF TITLE AND QUIET TITLE CLAIMS. 
IV. THE TRIAL COURT ERRED IN GRANTING EXCESSIVE 
DAMAGES TO THE DEFENDANT-APPELLEE. 
 
 
 
{¶12} In Delaware App. No. 26CAE070073, Hellas appeals the trial court’s July 9, 
2026 Judgment Entry, assigning the following as error: 
 
I. THE TRIAL COURT ERRED IN NOT GRANTING HELLAS AN 
AWARD OF REASONABLE ATTORNEYS’ FEES FOR HAVING TO 
RESPOND TO SORENSEN’S BAD FAITH FIRST COMPLAINT, WHICH 
SORENSEN ADMITTED TO FILING IN BAD FAITH.  THE ERROR IS 
REFLECTED IN THE TRIAL COURT’S ADOPTION OF THE 
MAGISTRATE’S JUNE 24, 2026 DECISION. TR 39.  
 
{¶13} This case comes to us on the accelerated calendar. App. R. 11.1, which governs 
accelerated calendar cases, provides, in pertinent part: 
 
(E) Determination and judgment on appeal. The appeal will be 
determined as provided by App. R. 11.1. It shall be sufficient compliance with 
App. R. 12(A) for the statement of the reason for the court's decision as to each 
error to be in brief and conclusionary form. The decision may be by judgment 
entry in which case it will not be published in any form. 
 
Standard of Review 
{¶14} Summary judgment proceedings present the appellate court with the unique 
opportunity of reviewing the evidence in the same manner as the trial court. Smiddy v. The 
 
 
Wedding Party, Inc. , 30 Ohio St.3d 35, 36 (1987) . As such, this Court reviews an award of 
summary judgment de novo. Grafton v. Ohio Edison Co., 77 Ohio St.3d 102, 105 (1996). 
{¶15} Civ.R. 56 provides summary judgment may be granted only after the trial court 
determines: 1) no genuine issues as to any material fact remain to be litigated; 2) the moving 
party is entitled to judgment as a matter of law; and 3) it appears from the evidence that 
reasonable minds can come to but one conclusion and viewing such evidence most strongly 
in favor of the party against whom the motion for summary judgment is made, that conclusion 
is adverse to that party. Temple v. Wean United, Inc., 50 Ohio St.2d 317 (1977). 
{¶16} The party moving for summary judgment bears the initial burden of 
demonstrating the absence of genuine issues of material facts concerning the essential 
elements of the nonmoving party's case. Dresher v. Burt, 75 Ohio St.3d 280, 292 (1996) . The 
moving party must support the motion by pointing to some evidence in the record of the type 
listed in Civil Rule 56(C) . Id. at 292 -293. However, the moving party need not support its 
motion for summary judgment with evidence negating his opponent's claim, but may simply 
point out that there is an absence of evidence to support the non-moving party's claim. Celotex 
Corp. v. Catrett, 477 U.S. 317, 325 (1986). 
{¶17} If the moving party satisfies this burden, then the non -moving party has the 
reciprocal burden to demonstrate a genuine issue for trial remains. Dresher, 75 Ohio St.3d at 
293. The nonmoving party may not rest upon the mere allegations or denials in her pleadings 
but must point to or submit evidence of the type specified in Civ.R. 56(C). Id.; Civ.R. 56(E). 
Types of evidence specified in Civ.R. 56 (C)  are “pleadings, depositions, answers to 
interrogatories, written admissions, affidavits, transcripts of evidence, and written stipulations 
of fact.” Civ.R. 56(C). 
 
 
Delaware App. No. 26CAE070071 
I 
{¶18} In its first assignment of error, Sorensen Construction contends the trial court 
erred in denying its motion for summary judgment on its breach of contract claim. 
{¶19} “A contract is generally defined as a promise, or a set of promises, actionable 
upon breach.”  JLP-Orange, LLC v. Tuller Square Northpointe, LLC , 2024-Ohio-2236, ¶ 15 (5th 
Dist.),  “Essential elements of a contract include an offer, acceptance, contractual capacity, 
consideration (the bargained for legal benefit and/or detriment), a manifestation of mutual 
assent and legality of object and of consideration.” (Citat

(Super. Ct. No. 37-2017-
00032731-CU-BT-NC) 

 APPEAL from an amended judgment of the Superior Court of San 
Diego County, Earl H. Maas, III, Judge. Affirmed. 
 Decker Law, James Decker, Griffin Schindler and Chris Jones for 
Defendant and Appellant. 
 Law Offices of Robert A. Ball, Robert A. Ball and John M. Donnelly for 
Plaintiffs and Respondents. 

 In the fourth appeal in this matter, The Crosby Clinic, LLC (Crosby 
Clinic or Clinic) seeks to shield assets from Glenn and Anastasia Kirkeby, 
judgment creditors and former business partners of the Clinic’s alter ego, 
2 

defendant Larry Burns. In this latest appeal, the Crosby Clinic challenges 
the trial court’s order granting the Kirkebys’ motion to amend the judgment 
to add the Crosby Clinic as a judgment debtor. Specifically, the Clinic argues 
Code of Civil Procedure section 580 barred the trial court from awarding 
damages against it because of its earlier default and because the complaint 
did not specify the amount of damages sought by the Kirkebys.1 The Clinic 
also contends the trial court erred by finding that its participation in the 
litigation was sufficient to support the court’s decision to add it as a judgment 
debtor. As we shall explain, we reject these arguments and affirm the 
amended judgment. 
FACTUAL AND PROCEDURAL BACKGROUND2 
A. Initial Proceedings 
 The Kirkebys first filed suit against Burns and various entities they 
alleged were under his control in September 2017. The lawsuit was also filed 
derivatively on behalf of MHCD, LLC, an entity jointly owned by the 
Kirkebys and Burns. Thereafter, Burns filed a demurrer to the complaint 
and sought to limit the Kirkebys’ discovery requests. Before the demurrer 
was resolved, in January 2018, the Kirkebys filed their First Amended 
Complaint (FAC) against Burns and the entities under his control, including 
the Crosby Clinic. The FAC alleged the Kirkebys started a drug and alcohol 

1 Subsequent undesignated statutory references are to the Code of Civil 
Procedure. 
2 Additional facts concerning the underlying dispute are set forth in our 
three prior opinions in this matter. (See Kirkeby v. Kahn (Sept. 17, 2024, 
D082333) [nonpub. opn.] (Kirkeby I), Kirkeby v. The Crosby Clinic, LLC 
(January 13, 2025, D083640 [nonpub. opn.] (Kirkeby II), and Kirkeby v. Kahn 
(June 9, 2025, D083388 [nonpub. opn.].) 
3 

abuse rehabilitation facility in 2002 shortly after meeting Burns, and that 
Burns claimed to be a licensed attorney and experienced business manager, 
who could help them operate the business. 
The FAC alleged that, unbeknownst to the Kirkebys, Burns 
misappropriated funds, business opportunities, and real estate (including the 
assets underlying this appeal) through his management of the rehabilitation 
center, known as the Crosby Center. In 2014, the Kirkebys discovered Burns 
was embezzling the business’s assets and contacted the Federal Bureau of 
Investigation.3 The FAC also alleged Burns and the various entities named 
in the complaint, including the Crosby Clinic, were each other’s alter egos.4 
The FAC asserted, there “is such a unity of interest and control between and 
among the Defendants, and each other, and Burns that their separate 
identities have ceased to exist, or never did exist” and that to “treat Burns 
and each entity Defendant (excepting the nominal Defendant, MHCD) as 
separate entities would perpetuate a fraud or result in gross injustice.” 
Burns and the entity defendants filed a demurrer to the FAC, which 
the trial court overruled. Burns and the Crosby Center filed separate 
answers on April 10, 2018. 

3 In their appellate brief, the Kirkebys assert that Burns is facing felony 
criminal charges in a case pending in San Diego Superior Court. 
4 The complaint named as the other entity defendants: The Crosby 
Clinic, LLC; Interlawus, LLC; AAE Alcohol Rehab Service Center; AAE 
Crosby Center; AAE Women Eating Disorder Center; Dream Catcher Detox 
Center, Inc.; KBY Properties, LLC; Crosby Recovery Foundation; AAA 
National Credit Reporting, Corp.; Internet Creative Marketing, Inc.; 
Stonegate Investment Group, LLC; Applied Psychology Systems, LLC; The 
Neuroscience Institute; and L Burns Research Institute. 
4 

In October 2019, MHCD filed a cross-complaint, which alleged similar 
claims against Burns, his then-wife Anne Kahn, and the same entities 
controlled by Burns named in the FAC. In addition, the complaint contained 
a cause of action for quiet title, asserting that Burns and the entities he 
controlled concealed, misappropriated, and diverted MHCD’s assets, 
resulting in the defendants wrongfully obtaining title to two properties in 
Escondido, one located on Camino De Las Lomas (Camino Property) and one 
located on Circle R Way (Circle R Property). MHCD sought adjudication of 
its ownership rights in the properties, and to quiet title in the two properties 
in its favor. MHCD also filed notices of pendency of action for the properties 
on October 24, 2019, with the San Diego County Recorder. 
The next day, October 25, 2019, the trial court struck the answers to 
the FAC of many of the entity defendants, including the Crosby Clinic, for 
failure to retain counsel. The court entered defaults against the entities the 
same day. 
In December 2019, MHCD, Burns, several of the named entities 
controlled by Burns, and Kahn entered stipulations for each property that 
enjoined transfer of the properties. Under the stipulations, the parties 
“agree[d] not to, and [were] enjoined from, encumbering, impairing, selling, 
transferring, conveying, or otherwise assigning the real estate and 
improvements ... during the pendency of this lawsuit.” In addition, the 
stipulations permitted the Crosby Clinic and NSI to seek refinancing of the 
Circle R Property, which faced foreclosure. MHCD agreed to dismiss its quiet 
title claim without prejudice and release the notices of pendency filed for each 
property to allow for the refinancing of the Circle R Property using the 
5 

Camino Property as collateral. The stipulations were signed into orders by 
the trial court on December 17, 2019.5 
In November 2020, despite the stipulated injunction orders precluding 
transfer or encumbrance of the properties, Burns encumbered the Camino 
Property with a deed of trust in the amount of $200,000. A little over a 
month later, on December 14, 2020, Burns conveyed title in the Camino 
Property from the Crosby Clinic to “Larry Burns Trustee of the Xanadau 
Dominican Irrevocable Trust – 2020” and conveyed title in the Circle R 
Property from NSI, another entity defendant controlled by Burns, to “Larry 
Burns Trustee of the Xanadau Dominican Irrevocable Trust – 2020.” This 
prompted the Kirkebys to record the stipulated injunction orders on the 
Camino and Circle R Properties with the county recorder on March 1, 2021. 
On November 3, 2021, the Kirkebys filed an application for an order to 
show cause (OSC) asserting Burns had violated the court’s stipulated 
injunction orders by transferring and encumbering the Camino Property and 
transferring the Circle R Property. After issuing the OSC, the court found 
Burns in contempt for violating the stipulated orders. On January 14, 2022, 
the court issued an order directing Burns to remove the encumbrance on the 
Camino Property and to reconvey the property back to the Crosby Clinic. 
B. Sanctions Against Burns & Additional Injunction Violations 
After Burns failed to reconvey the Camino Property back to the Crosby 
Clinic, on March 3, 2022, the Kirkebys and MHCD jointly moved for 
terminating sanctions against Burns based on his violations of the stipulated 

5 In January 2020, Burns and the entity defendants filed a demurrer to 
MHCD’s cross-complaint. The court overruled the demurrer, and Burns and 
the other defendants answered the cross-complaint in March 2020. 
6 

orders related to the two properties, and his failure to respond to their 
discovery requests. On May 2, 2022, the trial court granted the motions, 
issuing terminating sanctions against Burns “based on his disobedience of 
the court’s 1/14/22 order as to … reconveyance of the property” and Burns’s 
“repeated violations of orders.” The court struck Burns’s answers to the FAC 
and MHCD’s cross-complaint, deemed all matters alleged in the FAC and 
cross-complaint admitted, and entered defaults against Burns and in favor of 
the Kirkebys and MHCD. In addition, the court struck the answers of the 
entity defendants, including the Crosby Clinic, to MHCD’s cross-complaint 
because those entities had failed to retain counsel. The court also deemed 
admitted the allegations against the entity defendants. 
 On September 26, 2022, the Kirkebys and MHCD dismissed Kahn from 
the underlying proceedings without prejudice. Two days later, on September 
28, 2022, a judgment of dissolution was entered in the divorce proceedings 
between Kahn and Burns (Burns v. Kahn, Case No. 20FL010428N). The 
judgment incorporated a marital settlement agreement (MSA), which 
provided that title in the Camino and Circle R Properties would be 
transferred from the Crosby Clinic and NSI (which the judgment described as 
entities created and maintained by Burns) to Kahn free and clear of any 
interest of Burns, the Crosby Clinic, or NSI. The document stated the 
transfers are “[s]ubject to approval by the Court in related matters, including 
the Kirkeby Matter ....” The dissolution judgment also stated that the parties 
to the dissolution agreed that the Circle R and Camino Properties “shall be 
awarded to [Kahn] as her sole and separate property and the parties shall 
sign all documents necessary to transfer all two (2) properties to [Kahn].” 
On September 30, 2022, Burns, as manager of the Crosby Clinic, 
transferred title in the Camino Property to Kahn by quitclaim deed. 
7 

C. Damages Trial 
 On November 18, 2022, at a default prove-up hearing, the Kirkebys’ 
counsel requested the court vacate the hearing and set the case for trial 
solely on the issue of damages. The court granted the request, and entered 
an order on November 22, 2022, stating that in lieu of the prove-up hearing, 
the matter was set for trial “on the issue of damages only.” The order also 
modified the May 2, 2022 order issuing terminating sanctions against Burns 
to be “changed to issue sanctions on the issue of liability, [and] that the 
matters alleged in [the FAC] remain deemed admitted as to Burns.” The 
order further provided that “the defaults previously entered against Burns 
pursuant to the [May 2, 2022 order] be vacated, but that Burns be permitted 
to only present evidence at the upcoming trial on the issue of damages.” 
On January 5 and 30, 2023, the parties proceeded to a bench trial on 
the issue of damages for the claims asserted against Burns. After the trial, 
the court issued its final decision. The court noted Burns was previously 
found guilty of contempt and his liability was “established by motions well 
prior to trial.” The court found “the evidence regarding intentional transfer 
of assets, sometimes in direct contravention of existing court orders, [wa]s 
abundant” and awarded the Kirkebys “$3,037,216 in damages directly related 
to the intentional actions” of Burns and also awarded treble damages, for a 
total compensatory damage award of $9,111,648. The court denied the 
Kir

leads.caseName: SH Nashville, LLC v. FWREF Nashville Airport, LLC
leads.text:
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF TENNESSEE
AT NASHVILLE
October 1, 2025 Session
SH NASHVILLE, LLC ET AL. v. FWREF NASHVILLE AIRPORT, LLC
Appeal by Permission from the Court of Appeals
Chancery Court for Davidson County
No. 22-0569-BC Anne C. Martin, Chancellor
___________________________________
No. M2023-01147-SC-R11-CV
___________________________________
This case clarifies Tennessee’s standard for determining whether a contractual provision 
setting forth an amount of damages in the case of a breach should be enforced as liquidated 
damages or should be unenforceable as a penalty. Purchaser sought a declaratory judgment 
that a damages provision in a purchase and sale agreement for an existing Hilton-branded
hotel near the Nashville Airport was unenforceable. Seller responded that the plain 
language of the agreement established the enforceability of the provision because the 
parties agreed that actual damages would be difficult or impossible to ascertain and the 
liquidated sum was a reasonable estimate of damages. The trial court granted summary 
judgment in favor of Seller. The Court of Appeals reversed. We granted permission to 
appeal. We now clarify that when the parties to a contract expressly agree that actual 
damages would be difficult or impossible to ascertain and that their agreed upon liquidated 
sum is a reasonable estimate of damages, there is a presumption that the provision is 
enforceable as liquidated damages. To overcome this presumption, the party seeking to 
avoid enforcement of the provision must show, by a preponderance of the evidence, that 
the provision is actually an unenforceable penalty. Purchaser has not demonstrated any 
questions of fact to overcome the presumption. The judgment of the Court of Appeals is 
reversed, and the case is remanded to the Chancery Court for further proceedings consistent 
with this opinion.
Tenn. R. App. P. 11 Appeal by Permission; Judgment of the Court of Appeals 
Reversed; Remanded to the Trial Court
DWIGHT E. TARWATER, J., delivered the opinion of the Court, in which JEFFREY S. BIVINS,
C.J., and HOLLY KIRBY, SARAH K. CAMPBELL, and MARY L. WAGNER, JJ., joined.
Sarah B. Miller, Britt K. Latham, and Garrah Carter-Mason, Nashville, Tennessee, for the 
appellant, FWREF Nashville Airport, LLC.
11/16/2026

- 2 -
Donald Capparella, Michael Bressman, and Candi Henry, Nashville Tennessee, for the 
appellees, SH Nashville, LLC, and UNI Nashville Airport Hotel, LLC.
Emily Hamm Huseth, Michael F. Rafferty, Allison T. Gilbert, and William L. Brantley, 
Memphis, Tennessee, for the amici curiae, Belz Investco GP, Boyle Investment Company, 
LPI Memphis, Inc., Mid-America Apartment Communities, Inc., and Fogelman Properties, 
LLC.
OPINION
I. FACTUAL AND PROCEDURAL BACKGROUND
In October of 2019, FWREF Nashville Airport, LLC (“Seller”) entered into a 
purchase and sale agreement (the “Agreement”) with UNI Nashville Airport Hotel, LLC 
(“UNI” or “Purchaser”) for an existing Hilton-branded hotel near the Nashville airport.1
The Agreement set forth a purchase price of $79,000,000; an earnest money deposit of 
$1,750,000; and a closing date of January 3, 2020. The Agreement included a provision 
that stipulated, in relevant part, that
[d]ue to the fluctuation in land values, the unpredictable state of the economy 
and of governmental regulations, the fluctuating money market for real estate 
loans of all types, and other factors which directly affect the value and 
marketability of the Property, the parties recognize that it would be extremely 
difficult and impracticable, if not impossible, to ascertain with any degree of 
certainty the amount of damages which would be suffered by Seller in the 
event of Purchaser’s failure to perform its obligation to purchase the Property 
under this Agreement. Accordingly, the parties agree that a reasonable 
estimate of Seller’s damages in such event is the amount of Earnest Money, 
and if Purchaser defaults in any material respect in performing the obligation 
to purchase the Property under this Agreement to close . . . then Seller, as its 
sole remedy[2] therefor[e] . . . shall be entitled to immediately terminate this 
Agreement . . . and receive and retain the Earnest Money as liquidated 
damages[.]

1 Because UNI later assigned its interest to SH Nashville, LLC (“SH Nashville”) we refer to UNI 
and SH Nashville collectively and interchangeably as “Purchaser.”
2 The Agreement additionally provided in Section 6.3 that “[i]f any litigation or other enforcement 
proceeding is commenced in connection with this Agreement, then the prevailing party shall be entitled to 
receive payment of its reasonable attorneys’ fees and expenses and court costs from the other party (and in 
addition to any liquidated damages under Section 6.1).” 
- 3 -
The next month, the parties executed the first of twenty-four amendments to the 
Agreement. Each of the amendments stated the amount of an additional earnest money 
deposit or deposits, set out that the earnest money was deemed earned by Seller and non-
refundable to Purchaser, provided for either an extension of the closing date or extension 
of earnest money payment deadlines, and included a ratification provision.3 Amendment 2 
increased the purchase price to $79,750,000; and Amendment 3 further increased the 
purchase price to $82,125,000. Beginning with Amendment 7, Purchaser agreed that no 
further extensions for the delivery date of the earnest money or of the closing date would 
be granted “for any reason (including without limitation as a result of any factor relating to 
the current COVID-19 pandemic or related circumstance, it being understood that time is 
of the essence) and any further requests for extensions . . . shall result in immediate 
forfeiture of the Earnest Money to Seller.” Beginning with Amendment 14, executed on 
August 12, 2020, Howard Wu and Taylor Woods4 agreed “to join in as parties to the 
[Agreement] for the purposes of agreeing to the terms of Section 2.2(e)[5] of the
[Agreement].” In Amendment 23, UNI assigned the Agreement to SH Nashville, but UNI, 
Wu, and Woods were still to “remain fully liable for all obligations of Purchaser under the 
[Agreement].”6 Across the twenty-four amendments, Purchaser deposited a total of 
$18,917,500 in earnest money. 
On October 21, 2020, Purchaser learned that a new, Hilton-branded, on-airport hotel 
was scheduled to open in late 2023. According to Purchaser, this announcement was a 
surprise and led to concerns about the impact of the on -airport hotel on the ability to have 
a profitable Hilton hotel nearby. Still, the parties executed two additional amendments to 
the Agreement, including the final amendment on December 23, 2020. Purchaser was 
unable to close by the agreed upon date of January 11, 2021. Seller then notified Purchaser 
that the Agreement was automatically terminated. In May and June 2021, Purchaser sent 
letters to Seller indicating that Purchaser had acquired a replacement lender and asking 
Seller to either refund the earnest money or proceed with the sale. 

3 Beginning with Amendment 7, the ratification provision was titled “Ratification and No Other 
Changes.” 
4 Howard Wu and Taylor Woods are members of SH Nashville, LLC and UNI Nashville Airport 
Hotel, LLC. 
5 Section 2.2(e) provided that “Seller and Purchaser acknowledge and agree that if Purchaser does 
not terminate this Agreement as set forth in Section[] 1.3(g), the Earnest Money will be deemed earned by 
Seller and non-refundable to P urchaser for any reason except as otherwise specifically set forth in this 
Agreement.”
6 The assignment was again acknowledged in Amendment 24. 
- 4 -
Purchaser filed suit on April 22, 2022, seeking a declaratory judgment that Seller’s 
retention of the earnest money was an unenforceable penalty.7 Shortly after the initial 
complaint was filed, the suit was transferred to the “Davidson County Business Court Pilot 
Project.”8 After Purchaser filed its Second Amended Complaint, Seller counter-claimed for 
breach of contract and attorneys’ fees. As litigation proceeded, Purchaser sought discovery 
“related to those circumstances including, but not limited to, what [Seller’s] knowledge 
was of this new . . . on-airport hotel development during the process of [the] contract 
negotiations at issue” and “the circumstances surrounding the formation of the Agreement
and amendments thereto.” Seller opposed, arguing that the four corners of the Agreement 
and amendments were sufficient to decide whether the provision at issue was intended as 
an unenforceable penalty. The trial court found a stay of discovery appropriate. Seller then 
moved for summary judgment on Purchaser’s remaining declaratory judgment claim and 
Seller’s counterclaims for breach of contract and award of attorneys’ fees. 
The trial court granted Seller’s motion, finding no issues of material fact relating to 
the enforceability of the damages provision.It reasoned that “enforcement of this provision 
is appropriate because it was a reasonable prediction of the actual damages Seller would 
suffer if Purchaser[] breached the contract and does not violate public policy.” 
Accordingly, it dismissed Purchaser’s declaratory judgment claim and awarded Seller a 
judgment against Purchaser for breach of contract and attorneys’ fees. 
The Court of Appeals reversed the grant of summary judgment. The panel
determined that Seller had presented no evidence “upon which the trial court could base a 
determination as to whether the amount of liquidated damages ‘was a reasonable estimate 
of potential damages.’” SH Nash., 2024 WL 3880089, at *14 (quoting Guiliano v. Cleo, 
Inc., 995 S.W.2d 88, 100 (Tenn. 1999)). It reasoned that “[t]he language of the contracts 
stating that the parties agreed that the liquidated damages amounts were a reasonable 
estimate [was] not sufficient.” Id. We granted permission to appeal.

7 Purchaser also brought a claim for conversion. The trial court granted Seller’s motion to dismiss 
the conversion claim based upon the economic loss doctrine. The Court of Appeals reversed the dismissal 
of this claim. SH Nash., LLC v. FWREF Nash. Airport, LLC, No. M2023-01147-COA-R3-CV, 2024 WL 
3880089, at *5, *15 (Tenn. Ct. App. Aug. 20, 2024), perm. app. granted No. M2023-01147-SC-R11-CV, 
2025 WL 668823, at *1 (Tenn. Feb. 26, 2025). Seller now concedes that the economic loss doctrine does 
not bar the conversion claim but maintains that the enforceability of the liquidated damages provision is 
dispositive. We agree that the enforceability of the liquidated damages provision is dispositive. 
8 The Business Court Docket Pilot Project entered into Phase 2 by order of this Court on April 4, 
2017. Order Establishing the Davidson County Business Court Docket Pilot Project – Phase 2, ADM2017-
00638 (Tenn. Apr. 4, 2017). We explained that the specialized docket “provide[s] expedited resolution of 
business matters by a judge who is experienced and has expertise in handling complex business and 
commercial disputes, and who will continue to provide proactive, hands-on case management with realistic, 
meaningful deadlines and procedures adapted to the needs of each case for customized, quality outcomes.” 
Id.
- 5 -
II. STANDARD OF REVIEW
This Court reviews a trial court’s ruling on a motion for summary judgment de novo, 
with no presumption of correctness. Rye v. Women’s Care Ctr. of Memphis, MPLLC, 477 
S.W.3d 235, 250 (Tenn. 2015). Thus, we must make a “fresh determination of whether the 
requirements of Rule 56 of the Tennessee Rules of Civil Procedure have been satisfied.” 
Id. (citing Estate of Brown, 402 S.W.3d 193, 198 (Tenn. 2013)). Summary judgment is 
appropriate where “the pleadings, depositions, answers to interrogatories, and admiss ions 
on file, together with the affidavits, if any, show that there is no genuine issue as to any 
material fact and that the moving party is entitled to a judgment as a matter of law.”

leads.text:
[Cite as Dickard v. Jackson & Jackson, L.L.C., 2026-Ohio-4530.] 
 
 
 
 
IN THE COURT OF APPEALS 
 
TWELFTH APPELLATE DISTRICT OF OHIO 
 
BUTLER COUNTY 
 
 
 
 
 
DENNIS A. DICKARD, et al., 
 
     Appellees, 
 
vs. 
 
JACKSON & JACKSON, LLC, 
 
     Appellant. 
 
  
 
 
 
 
: 
 
: 
 
: 
 
: 
 
: 
 
: 
 
          CASE NO. CA2025-07-072 
 
OPINION AND 
JUDGMENT ENTRY 
11/16/2026 
 
 
 
CIVIL APPEAL FROM BUTLER COUNTY COURT OF COMMON PLEAS 
Case No. CV2023-10-2062 
 
 
 
 
Michael T. Gmoser, Butler County Prosecuting Attorney, and Stephen M. Wagner,  
Assistant Prosecuting Attorney, for appellees.  
 
Suder, LLC, and John P. Burleigh and Sean S. Suder, for appellant. 
 
 
____________ 
O P I N I O N 
 
 
 DONOVAN, J. 
{¶ 1} Appellant, Jackson & Jackson, LLC ("Jackson & Jackson") , appeals from 
the decision of the Butler County Court of Common Pleas which granted a Civ.R. 12(B)(6) 
Butler CA2025-07-072 
 
 - 2 - 
motion to dismiss filed by Appellees, Dennis A. Dickard and the Butler County Board of 
Commissioners. For the reasons discussed below, we sustain Jackson & Jackson's 
assignments of error in part, affirm the common pleas court's decision in part, reverse in 
part, and remand for further proceedings. 
I. Background Law 
{¶ 2} This appeal is more about the law than the particular facts of the case, 
turning on questions regarding whether various statutes and legal concepts were correctly 
applied by the trial court in the context of a case involving an alleged regulatory taking of 
property. To assist the reader, we will explain some of those statutes and legal concepts 
before describing the specific facts and the litigation history of this case. 
A. Takings Under Federal Law 
 
{¶ 3} The United States Constitution provides protections to property owners with 
respect to government takings of private property. The Fifth Amendment's Takings Clause 
states, "nor shall private property be taken for public use, without just compensation." 
U.S. Const., amend. V. This means that when the federal government takes private 
property, such as when it uses its eminent domain power, it owes just compensation for 
that taking to the owner of the property. The Fifth Amendment's Takings Clause does not 
only bind the federal government; it is also applicable to the States through the Fourteenth 
Amendment. Penn Cent. Transp. Co. v. City of New York, 438 U.S. 104, 123, fn. 3 (1978).  
{¶ 4} The United State Supreme Court has recognized that government 
regulation of property may constitute a taking of the property. Pennsylvania Coal Co. v. 
Mahon, 260 U.S. 393, 415 (1922). Such takings are known as "regulatory takings." "The 
general rule at least is that while property may be regulated to a certain extent, if 
regulation goes too far it will be recognized as a [regulatory] taking." Id. 
 
Butler CA2025-07-072 
 
 - 3 - 
B. Takings Under Ohio Law 
{¶ 5} Like the United States Constitution, the Ohio Constitution addresses 
property owners' rights with regard to takings of property by state government. Article I, 
Section 19 of the Ohio Constitution, titled "Eminent Domain," provides in relevant part,  
where private property shall be taken for public use, a 
compensation therefor shall first be made in money, or first 
secured by a deposit of money, and such compensation shall 
be assessed by a jury, without deduction for benefits to any 
property of the owner. 
 
Ohio Const., art.I, § 19. Though the title of Article I, Section 19 refers to "eminent domain" 
takings, that state constitutional provision also concerns regulatory takings. See TMS 
Ents., Ltd. v. Cleveland, 2026-Ohio-3229, ¶ 38-40 (8th Dist.).  
C. Types of Takings Claims 
{¶ 6} In Ohio state courts, a private property owner who believes a regulatory 
taking has taken place has several options on how to proceed. These options differ based 
on whether the property owner seeks compensation for the regulatory taking or future 
non-enforcement of the regulation that created the regulatory taking, and based on 
whether the property owner seeks enforcement of federal or state property rights. We will 
outline these options below. 
1. Federal Section 1983 Claim 
{¶ 7} First, if the property owner seeks compensation pursuant to his or her rights 
under the Fifth Amendment to the United States Constitution, the property owner may 
bring a claim under a federal statute, 42 U.S.C. 1983 ("Section 1983"). Section 1983 
provides a private cause of action against "every person who, under color of any statute, 
ordinance, regulation, custom, or usage, of any State. . . " deprives another of any rights 
secured by federal laws or the United States Constitution. 42 U.S.C. 1983; Wilder v. 
Virginia Hosp. Assn., 496 U.S. 498, 508 (1990); Maine v. Thiboutot, 448 U.S. 1, 4 (1980). 
Butler CA2025-07-072 
 
 - 4 - 
Courts have long recognized that Section 1983 provides a mechanism for asserting a 
claim for just compensation arising out of a taking under the Fifth Amendment. See 
Williamson Cty. Regional Planning Comm. v. Hamilton Bank of Johnson City , 473 U.S. 
172 (1985), overruled on other grounds by Knick v. Twp. of Scott, 588 U.S. 180 (2019). 
2. Petition for Writ of Mandamus 
{¶ 8} Second, if the property owner seeks compensation pursuant to his or her 
rights under Article I, Section 19 of the Ohio Constitution, the property owner may bring a 
petition for a writ of mandamus ordering appropriation proceedings under Chapter 163 of 
the Ohio Revised Code. In Ohio, "[a]n appropriation action is the procedural device 
provided by statute to carry out the state government's eminent domain power, otherwise 
known as a condemnation proceeding." Marchbanks v. JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. , 
2024-Ohio-5876, ¶ 18 (11th Dist.). The Ohio Supreme Court has held that a writ of 
mandamus is the "appropriate action to compel public authorities to institute appropriation 
proceedings where an involuntary taking of private property is alleged." State ex rel. 
Elsass v. Shelby Cty. Bd. of Commr., 2001-Ohio-1276, ¶ 21, citing State ex rel. BSW Dev. 
Group v. Dayton, 83 Ohio St.3d 338, 341 (1998); accord State ex rel. Shemo v. Mayfield 
Hts., 2002-Ohio-1627.  
3. Administrative Appeal 
{¶ 9} Third, rather than seeking compensation, a property owner may seek a use 
variance, appeal the denial of the variance to the court of common pleas, and then ask 
the common pleas court to reverse the denial of the use variance and/or find that the 
zoning regulation is unconstitutional as applied to the property. See Karches v. City of 
Cincinnati, 38 Ohio St.3d 12, 16 (1988). Such a finding of unconstitutionality would 
prevent future enforcement of the zoning regulation against the property.  
Butler CA2025-07-072 
 
 - 5 - 
{¶ 10} Because local zoning agencies may not decide constitutional issues, the 
property owner utilizing this procedure would not raise his or her constitutional argument 
for the first time until the matter reached the court of common pleas. In other words, the 
property owner would not be able to raise the constitutional argument before the zoning 
enforcement agency or the board of zoning appeals. 
4. Declaratory Judgment Action 
{¶ 11} Fourth, rather than seeking compensation, a property owner may ask a 
court to issue a declaratory judgment that the regulation is unconstitutional as applied to 
the property, and prohibiting the government from enforcing the regulation against the 
property on a going-forward basis. See Karches at 16; Driscoll v. Austintown Assoc., 42 
Ohio St.2d 263, 268 (1975). Such a declaratory judgment may be obtained pursuant to 
R.C. 2721.03, as discussed in more detail below, and may concern the constitutionality 
of a zoning regulation under either federal or state law. 
II. Factual and Procedural Background 
{¶ 12} This case was resolved on the pleadings pursuant to a Civ.R. 12(B)(6) 
motion to dismiss. The following facts are derived from Jackson & Jackson's counterclaim 
complaint, other pleadings, and any attachments, and are undisputed for purposes of this 
appeal. Haery v. Spaeth, 2025-Ohio-5801, ¶ 2 (12th Dist.) (in ruling on a pleading under 
Civ.R. 12[B][6] the trial court must presume that all factual allegations in the complaint are 
true and draw all reasonable inferences in favor of the nonmoving party.) 
A. Jackson & Jackson's Property Acquisition 
{¶ 13} The real estate at issue in this case ("the Property") consists of 
approximately nine acres of land and various improvements located at 5670 West 
Alexandria Road in Madison Township, Butler County, Ohio.  
Butler CA2025-07-072 
 
 - 6 - 
{¶ 14} The Property is and has been zoned R -1 "Suburban Residence District." 
While this zoning does not permit commercial uses, over the years the Property was used 
for a variety of non-residential, commercial functions. This included a golf driving range 
which opened in 2003. In 2009, a pizza business opened in conjunction with the driving 
range. And in 2018, a church began operating on the property. Notably, while the Property 
was not zoned for commercial use, the Butler County Auditor designated the Property as 
being for "Commercial" use. 
{¶ 15} On November 22, 2021, Jackson & Jackson acquired the Property from the 
previous owner for $270,000 through a general warranty deed.  
{¶ 16} Jackson & Jackson provides commercial electrical and emergency 
response services to help state and local governments restore power lines after storms 
or other events. Jackson & Jackson —aware of the Property's prior use for commercial 
purposes—acquired the Property with the intent to use it in conjunction with its business. 
After acquiring the Property, Jackson & Jackson began parking its trucks and other 
equipment on the Property's parking lot and using existing office space in one of the 
buildings for business functions. 
B. Zoning Violation Proceedings 
{¶ 17} Despite the prior use of the Property for commercial purposes, commercial 
use—and specifically Jackson & Jackson's commercial use—was not permitted under R-
1 District regulations. As a result, on or about May 9, 2023, the office of the Zoning 
Inspector for Butler County, Ohio served Jackson & Jackson with a notice of zoning 
violation and instructed Jackson & Jackson to cease and desist operating its business on 
the Property.  
{¶ 18} In response to the notice of violation, Jackson & Jackson applied for a use 
variance, seeking permission to park company vehicles and use the Property as an

administrative office. On August 17, 2023, the Butler County, Ohio Board of Zoning 
Appeals ("BZA") denied Jackson & Jackson's variance application. Jackson & Jackson 
did not appeal the BZA's decision to the Butler County Court of Common Pleas, but it 
continued operating its business on the Property.  
C. The County's Complaint for Injunctive Relief and 
   Jackson & Jackson's Answer and Counterclaim 
 
{¶ 19} In 2023, after Jackson & Jackson’s deadline to appeal the BZA decision to 
the common pleas court expired, Butler County Zoning Inspector Dennis Dickard filed a 
complaint against Jackson & Jackson in the Butler County Court of Common Pleas,

Resolution"). Jackson & Jackson filed an answer and a counterclaim complaint. Jackson 
& Jackson's counterclaim added the "County of Butler, Ohio" as a counterclaim -

Court of Appeals of Indiana | Opinion 26A-PL-490 | November 16, 2026 Page 1 of 21 
 
Pursuant to Ind. Appellate Rule 65(E), the trial court and parties shall not take any 
action in reliance upon this Opinion until it is certified. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
IN THE  
Court of Appeals of Indiana 
 
Steuben County, Indiana Plan Commission,  
Appellants-Respondents 
 
Todd and Sara Barile, Husband and Wife; Brian and Terri 
Richards, Husband and Wife; Jared and Michelle Widenhoefer, 
Husband and Wife; Kameron and Abby Meyer, Husband and 
Wife; Jeffrey and Lori Wagner, Husband and Wife; Ronald and 
Paula Laurent, Husband and Wife; Dorick Rudolph and 
Cynthia Baker, as Joint Tenants with Rights of Survivorship; 
Brian W. Strahm Revocable Living Trust, Dated August 7, 
2020; and Christopher A. and Nancy E. Graham,  
Husband and Wife, 
Appellants-Intervening-Respondents 
v. 
3rd Basin, LLC, 
Appellee-Petitioner 
Court of Appeals of Indiana | Opinion 26A-PL-490 | November 16, 2026 Page 2 of 21 
 
November 16, 2026 
Court of Appeals Case No. 
26A-PL-490 
Appeal from the Steuben Circuit Court 
The Honorable Jeremy T. Musser, Judge 
Trial Court Cause No. 
76C01-2505-PL-265 
Opinion by Chief Judge Tavitas 
Judges Bradford and Felix concur. 
Tavitas, Chief Judge. 
Case Summary 
[1] The Steuben County Plan Commission (“Plan Commission”) and a group of 
intervening neighboring property owners (“Intervenors”) appeal the trial court’s 
grant of a petition for judicial review filed by 3rd Basin, LLC (“3rd Basin”).  
This litigation concerns the Plan Commission’s conditional grant of 3rd Basin’s 
application for primary approval of a subdivision plat.  3rd Basin argued that 
the Plan Commission erred by imposing a condition on the grant of the 
application and filed a petition for judicial review.  We conclude that the trial 
court erred by granting 3rd Basin’s petition for judicial review.  Accordingly, we 
reverse. 
Court of Appeals of Indiana | Opinion 26A-PL-490 | November 16, 2026 Page 3 of 21 
 
Issue 
[2] The Plan Commission and Intervenors raise two issues, which we consolidate 
and restate as whether the trial court erred by granting 3rd Basin’s petition for 
judicial review.   
Facts  
[3] This litigation involves the Plan Commission’s conditional approval for 3rd 
Basin’s proposed subdivision primary plat on the shores of Crooked Lake in 
Steuben County.  As the matter turns on the interpretation of relevant statutes 
and ordinances, we begin by setting out the relevant Steuben County 
Ordinances. 
A.  Relevant Steuben County Ordinances 
1.  Steuben County Subdivision Control Ordinance  
[4] The Steuben County Subdivision Control Ordinance (“Subdivision Control 
Ordinance”) provides that the Plan Commission has “all the powers and duties 
with respect to primary and secondary plats of subdivisions[.]”  Appellants’ 
App. Vol. III p. 107 (Preamble and Enacting Clause).  The Subdivision Control 
Ordinance “shall be held to be the minimum requirements for the protection of 
the public health, safety, and general welfare . . . .”  Id. at 107 (Preamble and 
Enacting Clause) (emphasis added); see also id. at 125 (Section 8.1(a)).  In 
addition to the requirements established in the Subdivision Control Ordinance, 
“all subdivision plats shall comply with” all applicable state and local statutory 
provisions and “[t]he County Zoning Ordinance[.]”  Id. at 109 (Section 
Court of Appeals of Indiana | Opinion 26A-PL-490 | November 16, 2026 Page 4 of 21 
 
3.1(a)(2)).  Where any provision of the Subdivision Control Ordinance 
“imposes restrictions [different] from those imposed by any other provision of 
this Ordinance, any other ordinance, rule or regulation, or other provision of 
Law, whichever provisions are more restrictive or impose higher standards, 
shall control.”  Id. at 125 (Section 8.1(b)(1)) (emphasis added).  Section 3.1(b) of 
the Subdivision Control Ordinance provides: “Plat approval may be withheld if 
a subdivision is not in conformity with the above guides and requirements, or 
with the policies and purposes of these Regulations.”  Id. at 109.   
[5] In general, the approval process for a major subdivision, which is at issue here, 
requires several steps.  First, an application for primary approval of a 
preliminary plat is submitted, and public hearings are held.  The Subdivision 
Control Ordinance provides that the Plan Commission shall “grant primary 
approval, primary approval with conditions, disapprove the plat, or table the 
plat for more information.”  Appellants’ App. Vol. III p. 61.  If the Plan 
Commission approves the primary plat, construction plans are submitted, and 
the Plan Director “shall immediately refer these plans to the appropriate 
agencies of the participating jurisdictions for review.”  Id.  If the construction 
plans are approved by the appropriate agencies, an application for secondary 
approval of the plat is submitted and considered by the Plan Commission.  The 
secondary approval request must “[t]otally comply with the Ordinance and 
terms and conditions of primary approval.”  Id. at 62.   
Court of Appeals of Indiana | Opinion 26A-PL-490 | November 16, 2026 Page 5 of 21 
 
2.  Steuben County Zoning Ordinance 
[6] 3rd Basin’s property at issue here is zoned Lake Residential.  The Steuben 
County Zoning Ordinance (“Zoning Ordinance”) establishes the following 
regarding this zoning district: 
The LR, Lake Residence District, is established to include 
residential neighborhoods in the proximity of bodies of water.  
These areas are characterized by environmental sensitivity and 
are subject to heavy recreational use.  Uses in the LR District are 
limited to residential and certain water-related and recreational-
related uses compatible with both the nearby development and 
the local, environmentally sensitive land.  The regulations of this 
district are intended to ensure infill development is consistent 
with the character of established lakefront neighborhoods, is 
compatible with the size, scale, setback, and architectural 
character of surrounding homes, does not overbuild small lots 
and minimizes impacts to views. 
Id. at 70. 
[7] In the Lake Residential district, common use lake access lots require “Special 
Exception approval” from the Board of Zoning Appeals (“BZA”).  Id. at 70-71.  
Section 17.01 of the Zoning Ordinance provides: “A use listed in a zoning 
district as a special exception use may only be established or expanded with the 
approval of the Board of Zoning Appeals (BZA) following the procedures and 
requirements of this chapter.”  Id. at 74.  Section 9.10(b) concerns common use 
lake access lots and provides: 
Court of Appeals of Indiana | Opinion 26A-PL-490 | November 16, 2026 Page 6 of 21 
 
Common Use Riparian/Lake Access Lots 
(1)  The intent of this provision is to minimize the impacts of 
Back lot Development on the Shoreline.  Further, it is the intent 
of this provision to: 
a.  discourage the funneling of lake access for multiple 
residences through narrow access points, 
b.  establish a balanced and orderly relationship between 
development and the amount of Shoreline available for use 
by residents, and 
c.  assure responsible “lake access” for Lakefront 
Development. 
(2)  This section shall apply to lakefront or back lot development, 
including, lake front access points, lake front recreational areas, 
beaches, parks, [and] playgrounds that have been designated as a 
common area or access point, in all zoning districts.  This section 
shall apply to common areas lakefront or back lot developments 
created as part of a residential subdivision . . . . 
(3)  Where a parcel of land contiguous to a natural body of water 
is proposed for residential development, a commonly owned area 
bordering on the body of water may be dedicated for recreational 
purposes. 
 
* * * * * 
Court of Appeals of Indiana | Opinion 26A-PL-490 | November 16, 2026 Page 7 of 21 
 
(4)  Common use waterfront lots shall not be used for public 
marinas, public beaches or commercial recreational use operated 
for profit. 
(5)  The design, operation and use of the common waterfront lot 
shall not impair the natural appearance of the land, overcrowd 
the lake surface or produce unreasonable noise or annoyance to 
surrounding properties. 
* * * * * 
Id. at 72.   
B.  3rd Basin’s Proposed Plat Application 
[8] 3rd Basin owns 23.63 acres in Steuben County near Crooked Lake 
(“Property”), and the Property is zoned Lake Residential.  3rd Basin desires to 
subdivide the Property into a thirty-two-lot major subdivision entitled Shores of 
Crooked Lake.  The lots would share access to the lake through a single access 
point, designated as “Common Area A,” together with a large, proposed pier.  
Appellants’ App. Vol. II p. 33.  Only two of the lots would have direct lake 
access.  Id.  The proposed plat presents a “funneling” configuration in which 
lake access for the non-waterfront lots is concentrated to one common access 
point. 
[9] On March 6, 2025, 3rd Basin filed an application with the Plan Commission for 
primary approval of a preliminary subdivision plat.  A hearing was held before 
the Plan Commission on April 2, 2025.  Funneling was a concern raised by 
remonstrators.  During the hearing, 3rd Basin’s counsel stated: 
Court of Appeals of Indiana | Opinion 26A-PL-490 | November 16, 2026 Page 8 of 21 
 
We were advised today that there would be needed a special 
exception for the common use dock.  We understand that.  That 
was the first we had heard of it.  But that is the part of the 
ordinance where all of your anti-funneling provisions are in, and 
so those are the criteria upon which that special exception is to be 
reviewed.  This was never flagged before really earlier as an extra 
step, but we’re willing to go through with that. 
Id. at 133.  Ultimately, at the hearing, the Plan Commission approved the 
primary plat on the condition that 3rd Basin obtain a special exception as 
required by the Zoning Ordinance.  The Plan Commission later issued the 
following written findings: 
5.  The Plat submitted by 3rd Basin, LLC, complies with the 
improvement standards of the Steuben County Subdivision 
Control Ordinance and there has been no evidence presented that 
they are not in compliance. 
6.  The Petitioners, 3rd Basin, LLC, have consented to a special 
exception for a common-use dock. 
The Steuben County Plan Commission gives primary plat 
approval conditioned upon 3rd Basin, LLC, obtaining a special 
exception for a common-use dock. 
Id. at 186-88. 
[10] In May 2025, 3rd Basin filed its petition for judicial review, challenging the 
condition imposed by the Plan Commission.  3rd Basin argued that Indiana 
Code Section 36-7-4-702 did not allow the Plan Commission to impose the 
special exception condition on the primary plat and that it was prejudiced by 
Court of Appeals of Indiana | Opinion 26A-PL-490 | November 16, 2026 Page 9 of 21 
 
the Plan Commission’s decision.  Intervenors filed a motion to intervene, which 
the trial court granted.  Additionally, the trial court took judicial notice of the 
Zoning Ordinance and the Subdivision Control Ordinance in existence as of 
March 6, 2025.   
[11] After briefing and a hearing on 3rd Basin’s petition for judicial review, the trial 
court granted the petition.  The trial court found: 
40.  As noted above, the Plan Commission stated in its findings 
that 3rd Basin complied with the plat procedures for primary 
approval.  The Plan Commission further found that the 
submitted plat complied with the improvement standards of the 
Subdivision Control Ordinance, and that no evidence was 
presented that 3rd Basin was not in compliance. 
41.  The Court agrees with 3rd Basin that the plain reading of IC 
§ 36-7-4-702(d) indicates the General Assembly intended to limit 
the conditions that may be placed upon a primary plat approval 
to the enumerated subsections.  “May specify” is construed to

leads.caseName: K. Scott v. Bowmanstown Borough Authority
leads.text:
IN THE COMMONWEALTH COURT OF PENNSYLVANIA 

Kara Scott : 
 : 
 v. : No. 18 C.D. 2025 
 : Submitted: April 13, 2026 
Bowmanstown Borough Authority, : 
 Appellant : 

BEFORE: HONORABLE RENÉE COHN JUBELIRER, President Judge 
 HONORABLE MATTHEW S. WOLF, Judge 
 HONORABLE BONNIE BRIGANCE LEADBETTER, Senior Judge 

OPINION NOT REPORTED 

MEMORANDUM OPINION BY 
PRESIDENT JUDGE COHN JUBELIRER FILED: November 16, 2026 

 The Bowmanstown Borough Authority (Authority) appeals from the January 
19, 2024 Decision and Verdict (Verdict) of the Court of Common Pleas of Carbon 
County (common pleas) , entered after a non -jury trial , wherein common pleas 
entered judgment for Kara Scott (Scott) and directed the Authority to return to Scott 
a $3 ,000.00 tapping fee (tapping fee) 1 and any additional charges assessed in 

1 This Court has described a tapping fee as follows: 

When a new residential or commercial customer desires (or is required) to connect 
to a municipal authority ’s sewer system, the municipal authority is authorized, 
pursuant to the [Municipality Authorities Act (MAA), 53 Pa.C.S. §§ 5601 -5623], 
to charge a “tapping fee” to recoup its capital costs incurred in constructing the 
particular facilities required to provide service to the new customer. The tapping 
fee is a one-time charge for access to the sewer system; it is not to be confused with 
a user fee, which is a separate ongoing charge for actual use of the system. 

J. Buchanan Assocs., LLC v. Univ. Area Joint Auth., 231 A.3d 1089, 1091 (Pa. Cmwlth. 2020). 
2 
connection with the tapping fee .2 In the Verdict, common pleas determined the 
Authority’s assessment of an additional equivalent dwelling unit (EDU)3 to Scott’s 
residential property, located at 422 Ore Street, Bowmanstown, Carbon County (the 
Property), and the assessment of the tapping fee and additional charges , was 
improper because the express and unambiguous language of the Authority’s 
Resolution 2005-02 (the Resolution) , upon which the Authority relied, was 
inapplicable to the Property and the facts underlying this case, and the Authority’s 
interpretation of the Resolution was inconsistent with the Resolution’s unambiguous 
language. Upon careful review of the record and the law, because we hold the 
Resolution’s language is clear and unambiguous and does not apply to Scott and the 
Property under the present factual circumstances, we affirm. 

I. BACKGROUND 
 The relevant facts underlying this case are not in dispute. In 1999, the 
previous owners of the Property entered into a written agreement (the Agreement) 
with the Borough of Bowmanstown (Borough), wherein the Property was converted 
from a building containing two EDUs for sanitary sewage purposes into a building 
with one EDU. (Verdict, Findings of Fact (FOF) ¶¶ 10-11; Reproduced Record 

2 The Authority ’s Notice of Appeal , Scott’s brief, and common pleas ’ opinion filed 
pursuant to Pennsylvania Rule of Appellate Procedure 1925(a), Pa.R.A.P 1925(a), identify the 
order on appeal as common pleas’ order of December 13, 2024, denying the Authority’s motion 
for post-trial relief. The Authority in its brief , however, correctly identifies the Verdict as the 
determination in question. For clarity, we note that an “[a]ppeal lies from the judgment entered 
and not the denial of post -trial motions, [] and a verdict d[oes] not become final for purposes of 
appeal until properly reduced to and entered as a formal judgment under [Pennsylvania Rule of 
Civil Procedure 227.4,] Pa.R.C[iv.]P. [] 227.4.” Mitchell v. Milburn, 199 A.3d 995, 999 n.2 (Pa. 
Cmwlth. 2018) (quotation marks and citations omitted). Thus, the Court construes the Authority’s 
Notice of Appeal as a timely appeal of the Verdict. 
3 An EDU “is a unit of measurement for volume of sewage flow, and typically one EDU 
will correspond to one residence.” J. Buchanan Assocs., LLC, 231 A.3d at 1091 n.1. 
3 
(R.R.) at 17a-21a.) This conversion was conditioned on the removal of all cooking 
facilities within the Property other than the remaining kitchen , a condition the 
previous owners satisfied. (FOF ¶ 10; R.R. at 18a.) The Agreement further stated, 
in part, that the “[o]wner acknowledges that a change of use or additional sewage 
discharge may require [o]wner or [o]wner’s heirs, executors, trustees, successors or 
assigns, to pay the Borough a fee based upon the number of additional [EDUs] to be 
operated at the” Property. (R.R. at 18a (emphasis added).) There is no dispute as to 
the validity of the Agreement. 
 Since 2004, Scott has owned and resided at the Property . (Id. at 56a.) At 
some point in early -to-mid-2021, Scott made cosmetic upgrades to part of the 
Property, converting a bedroom, sitting room, and bathroom on the first floor with 
plans to begin hosting guests through the Airbnb platform. (FOF ¶¶ 12-13; R.R. at 
57a-58a.) In June 2021, Scott submitted a home occupation application /permit 
(application) seeking to use the first floor of the Property as a bed and breakfast, but 
this application was denied by a Borough zoning officer via letter, in part, because 
the zoning officer believed a kitchenette constituted a cooking facility. (FOF ¶¶ 14-
15; R.R. at 120a.) The letter further instructed Scott to seek a variance for the bed 
and breakfast. (FOF ¶ 16; R.R. at 120a.) Scott appealed this denial to the Borough’s 
Zoning Hearing Board (ZHB) and sought a variance and special exception , which, 
after a public hearing was held and testimony was taken, the ZHB through a written 
decision granted Scott.4 (FOF ¶ 17; R.R. at 24a-28a.) 

4 The ZHB determined that the presence of a dorm refrigerator, coffee pot, small 
microwave, and toaster did not constitute a cooking facility , that Scott’s use of the Property did 
not alter the character of the neighborhood , and that use of the Property as a bed and breakfast 
would not impact the community or neighborhood any more than when Scott’s sons previously 
occupied the first floor of the Property . (FOF ¶ 18; R.R. at 27a.) The ZHB’s grant of a special 
exception was conditioned on the number of occupants in the bed and breakfast not exceeding two 
(Footnote continued on next page…) 
4 
 Following the ZHB’s decision, the Authority’s solicitor sent Scott a letter (the 
EDU Assessment Determination). (FOF ¶ 20; R.R. at 89a.) The EDU Assessment 
Determination explained that under Section 1.9(c)1.(F) of the Resolution , the 
application and approval of the special exception created a new and separate 
business use/non -residential use of the Property, thus, subjecting Scott and the 
Property to the assessment of an additional EDU and the accompanying tapping fee. 
(FOF ¶ 21; R.R. at 90a.) 
 Scott paid the tapping fee and other charges out of caution and filed a 
declaratory judgment action with common pleas challenging the Authority’s EDU 
Assessment Determination. (FOF ¶ 25.) Common pleas held a bench trial, where it 
took testimony from Scott, the only witness . After the bench trial, in the written 
Verdict, common pleas made, in relevant part, the following additional findings of 
fact: 

22. The Authority based its decision that the [Property] would be 
assessed an additional EDU on Section 1.9(c) 1.(F) of [the] Resolution 
. . . which provides: Computing a Non -Residential Multi-Unit EDU. 
When more than one commercial establishment is contained in a 
building, each business establishment will be considered one dwelling 
unit if the commercial establishment contains a separate toilet facility. 

23. The [Property] does not have more than one commercial 
establishment. 

people. (FOF ¶ 18; R.R at 28a.) It does not appear from the record that the ZHB’s decision was 
appealed to common pleas and, therefore, it became final and binding. See Narberth Borough 
v. Lower Merion Township , 915 A.2d 626, 637 (Pa. 2007) (noting that for land use appeals, the 
Pennsylvania Municipalities Planning Code, Act of July 31, 1968, P.L. 805, as amended, 53 P.S. 
§§ 10101-11202, “ creates a period of time during which all appeals must be filed and it 
specifies a triggering event, the mailing or other direct communication of the written decision” ) 
(emphasis added); First Ave. Partners v. City of Pittsburgh Plan. Comm’n, 151 A.3d 715, 722 (Pa. 
Cmwlth. 2016) (“[Z]oning decisions are not final until a written decision is issued, and until a 
written decision is issued, there is no order to appeal.”). 
5 
24. The [Property] is not: a non-residential improved property, Section 
1.9(c)l.(C); a residential multi -unit facility, Section 1.9(c)l.(E); or a 
non-residential multi-unit facility, Section 1.9(c)1.(F). 

25. As a consequence of the Authority’s determination that the 
[Property] would be assessed an additional EDU, [Scott] has paid an 
additional tapping fee of three thousand dollars ($3 ,000.00) and 
additional fees of twenty dollars and seventy -five cents ($20.75) per 
month. 

(FOF ¶¶ 22-25). Common pleas then made the following conclusions of law (COL): 

1. There is no provision within [the] Resolution . . . which permits the 
Authority to determine that the [Property] has two (2) EDUs. 

2. The rules of statutory construction are applicable to both statutes, 
ordinances, and resolutions. In re Appeal of Edwin R. Thompson, 896 
A.2d 659, 669 (Pa. Cmwlth. 2006). 

3. The words of [the] Resolution . . . are clear and free of all ambiguity 
and, as such, the letter of the [R]esolution is not to be disregarded under 
the pretext of pursuing its spirit. [Section 1921(b) of the Statutory 
Construction Act of 1972 (SCA),] 1 Pa.C.S. § 1921(b). 

4. Since the language of [the] Resolution . . . is unambiguous, statutory 
interpretation is not necessary in this instance. Commonwealth 
v. McClintic, 909 A.2d 1241, 1246 (Pa. 2006). 

5. Where an administrative interpretation is inconsistent with the 
resolution itself, or where the resolution ’s meaning is unambiguous, 
such an interpretation carries little or no weight. Terminato v. Pa. Nat’l 
Ins. Co. , 645 A.2d 1287, 1293 (Pa. 1994); Velocity Express v. Pa. 
Hum[.] Rel[s.] Comm’n, 853 A.2d 1182, 1185 (Pa. Cmwlth. 2004). 

6. Although courts often defer to an agency’s interpretation of the 
statutes it administers, when convinced that the agency’s interpretation 
is unwise or erroneous, that deference is unwarranted. Rosen v. Bureau 
of Pro[. &] Occupational Aff[s.], State Architects Licensure B[d.], 763 
A.2d 962, 968 (Pa. Cmwlth. 2000). 

7. The Authority’s interpretation of [the] Resolution . . . is inconsistent 
with the Resolution itself and is, therefore, erroneous as applied to 
[Scott]. 
6 

8. There is no provision within [the] Resolution . . . which concerns 
itself with those situations in which a residential dwelling has a business 
within the [Property]. 

9. Section 1.9(c)l.(F) of [the] Resolution . . . is inapplicable to the facts 
in this case in that the plain language of this section does not concern 
itself with a situation in which a residential dwelling has a business 
within the [Property]. 

(Verdict, COL ¶¶ 1-9). In sum, common pleas concluded that the Resolution did not 
permit the Authority to assess an additional EDU on the Property or an additional 
tapping fee and directed the Authority to reimburse Scott accordingly. 
 The Authority filed a motion for post -trial relief, seeking to modify the 
Verdict based on what the Authority thought were erroneous findings of fact and 
conclusions of law made by common pleas and further seeking entry of judgment in 
favor of the Authority. (R.R. at 184a -87a.) By order dated December 13, 2024, 
common pleas denied the motion for post -trial relief , and the Authority timely 
appealed to this Court. By order dated July 22, 2025, this Court instructed the 
Authority to praecipe common pleas for an entry of judgment. See Scott 
v. Bowmanstown Borough Auth. (Pa. Cmwlth., No . 18 C.D. 2025, filed July 22, 
2025). As noted above, because an appeal properly lies from the entry
